organization.name: Protection Dogs GR
organization.description: A small, trainer-led Belgian Malinois protection dog program based in Greece, developing a limited number of working-line dogs at a time for individuals and families with genuine protection needs.

mainEntity.name: What makes your breeding program different?

acceptedAnswer.text: I keep the breeding program small and selective. Working ability, nerve, health, pedigree depth, and complementary traits between sire and dam all matter. The goal is not to produce more litters; it is to give the training program better raw material to work with.

mainEntity.name: How do you test your dogs' working ability?

acceptedAnswer.text: Every dog is tested under real, layered pressure - not a single controlled scenario, but compound, unpredictable stress that reflects what a genuine security situation actually looks like. What I look for is clarity under pressure, commitment, how quickly the dog recovers and re-engages, and whether it returns to control when the situation changes. These are not standard protection dogs - they are working dogs developed for genuine security needs.

mainEntity.name: What level of handler experience is required?

acceptedAnswer.text: These dogs require experienced handling. They are true working Malinois with strong drives - not standard family pets. Handlers must be committed to maintaining training and managing a high-drive working dog. I provide handler training and ongoing support to support a successful integration.

mainEntity.name: What training do your dogs receive?

acceptedAnswer.text: Development starts with early handling and environmental work, followed by socialization, obedience, drive development, protection foundations, progressive scenario work, final evaluation, and handler integration. Every dog follows the same core standard; later work can be adapted to the future handler and environment.

mainEntity.name: What health testing do you perform?

acceptedAnswer.text: Every breeding prospect undergoes extensive health testing including hip and elbow certification, comprehensive DNA screening, and full veterinary examination. I only breed dogs that meet my strict health and working requirements to maintain the standard of the program.

mainEntity.name: What is your client selection process?

acceptedAnswer.text: I carefully evaluate each potential client to make sure they understand the commitment required for a true working dog. This includes assessing handler experience, security needs, and ability to maintain training. These dogs are for serious protection needs and require experienced handling.

mainEntity.name: How long is the waiting period?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no fixed waiting period because availability depends on the dogs currently in development and how many I can train properly at one time. Contact me to discuss the dogs currently in development and upcoming availability.

intro.h3: A Small Program Built Around the Dog
paragraphs: Protection Dogs GR is a small working-dog program focused on developing capable, stable Malinois for real protection work. I start with proven working genetics, then evaluate what each dog actually shows through development and training.

The goal is not to make a dog look impressive in a demonstration. The goal is to develop a dog that can work with intensity, stay clear-headed under pressure, and return to control when the situation changes.

about.pullQuote: A bloodline gives you potential. The trainer determines what becomes of it.

paragraphs: Protection Dogs GR is a small, trainer-led working-dog program. I breed, raise and develop a limited number of Malinois so I can remain directly involved with each dog from early development through final placement.

I want commitment without loss of clarity, stability outside the work, and the ability to recover and return to control when pressure ends. Not every dog belongs in protection work, and I do not place one simply because it can perform a demonstration.

Because the program is small, clients deal directly with me throughout the process. When a dog is reserved during development, the future owner can follow its progress, ask questions, receive current photos and videos, and gradually become part of the dog's preparation before handover.
I only work with a small number of dogs at a time because I train and evaluate them directly. Availability is therefore limited by training capacity, not by artificial scarcity.
If you want to discuss a current or future dog, contact me directly:

future.name: Future Availability
future.paragraph: The program remains deliberately small. If you want a future dog, I'd encourage you to speak with me early — when a suitable dog makes the program and the match is right, reservation can begin during development rather than waiting until final handover. That gives you the opportunity to follow the dog, build a relationship with the process, and spread payments across the development period.

video.ariaLabel: Bobo, Belgian Malinois protection dog in development

slides.p: Bobo has never needed to be talked into confidence — it's simply how he came into the world. His drive is the same: strong and natural, nothing manufactured. He's a hard biter, and whatever the work is on a given day, he's willing to do it.

Off duty, Bobo is genuinely good company — comfortable and social around children and other animals, not just tolerant of them. A dog capable of real protection work still has to know how to be a dog the rest of the time, and he does.

I bred Bobo myself and have hand-raised him from day one, the same as every dog that comes through here. Dark-coated, a genuinely nice head, and built up gradually rather than pushed. He also loves the sea — swimming is one of his favorite things in the world.

slides.h4: Built for Someone Who Needs a Real Protector
slides.p: Bobo is shaping up to be a strong, serious dog — not a hobby companion, but one meant for someone who actually needs real protection. Every part of how he's been raised has been in service of that.

paragraphs: For many clients, the relationship begins before the dog is finished. When a suitable dog is reserved during development, I keep the future owner close to the process — current photos, short videos, and honest training updates, so they can watch the dog grow and follow the progression toward handover.

The updates are intentionally real rather than produced like advertising. Much of the day-to-day training is simply filmed as it happens, the same way I'd film it for my own review. The point isn't to create content — it's to let the future owner see their dog honestly over time.

training.intro: A five-phase development system built around a simple principle: drive and self-control are developed separately, then brought together deliberately.

phases.title: Early Development
phases.intro: Development begins in the first days of life. Early handling and controlled stimulation are used to build a stronger foundation for later environmental confidence and stress resilience.

Controlled exposure to textures, surfaces, and sensory experiences
Continuous evaluation of genetic expression and aptitude indicators

phases.title: Socialization
phases.intro: During this critical socialization period, I follow structured exposure work to develop confident, stable dogs capable of functioning in diverse environments.

features.p: Controlled exposure to various people, animals, and environments
Systematic exposure to diverse surfaces, sounds, and scenarios
Foundation work for specialized detection capabilities

phases.title: Foundation
phases.intro: This phase establishes core obedience and introduces foundational protection concepts, creating the framework for advanced capabilities.

features.p: Establishing reliable command response in all environments
Channeling genetic drives into focused working capability

phases.title: Protection Development
phases.intro: Protection work becomes progressively more demanding through varied people, locations, surfaces, distractions, and pressure. The purpose is to test whether the dog can keep thinking as the work becomes harder.

phases.intro: The final phase is about proving the dog consistently, identifying any remaining weaknesses, and teaching the future handler how to maintain the work correctly.

paragraphs: Intensity alone tells me very little.

I want to see what happens when pressure becomes layered, unfamiliar and unpredictable. The dog must remain committed without losing clarity, and it must be capable of returning to a controlled state when the situation changes.

Recovery is particularly important to me. I watch how quickly a dog can process stress, re-engage and return to productive work. That tells me considerably more than intensity in a familiar training setup.

I film training sessions so I can review both the dog's performance and my own handling. The purpose is simple: evaluate honestly, identify weaknesses early and make better decisions as the dog develops.

Breeding decisions in my program go beyond a health clearance and a good pedigree on paper. I look for genuine complementary drive character between sire and dam — lines that fill in each other's gaps rather than stacking the same strengths and the same risks. I work closely with the math behind it too: coefficient-of-inbreeding calculations across the full pedigree, not just the first two or three generations, so I understand exactly what I'm concentrating and what I'm diluting before a breeding decision is made.

I've also brought in outside lines deliberately — including dogs from rare, closed Belgian working bloodlines used by special forces and law enforcement programs — specifically to strengthen genetic depth rather than simply chase a name on paper. It is a slower way to breed and develop dogs, but it gives me more control over what I am producing and why each breeding is made.

Every dog I raise goes through the same training system, refined through hands-on work and continuous evaluation. The system is consistent, but the trainer still has to read the individual dog and make the right decisions at the right time.

Foundation comes before pressure. Before a young dog ever sees real pressure equipment, I build frustration tolerance the right way — through structured chase-and-release work that teaches a dog how to want something intensely and still stay thinking. Skip this step, and you get a dog that's explosive but can't be brought back down. I don't skip it.

Calm is the anchor, not the exception. I train every dog to return to a settled, possessive calm as its default state — even mid-grip, even under stress. A protection dog's job isn't to stay wound up; it's to know exactly when to switch states, and switch back just as fast.
The dogs are not developed in an isolated commercial environment. They are part of my day-to-day life while they grow and train.
My family is naturally around parts of that process, which gives me additional opportunities to observe how a dog settles, responds to normal household activity, and behaves outside formal training.

blocks.html: These dogs are matched carefully, including with:

items: People protecting a family or home
Business or property owners with genuine security concerns
People facing a specific threat or security problem
Experienced handlers looking for a serious working dog

blocks.html: The right placement depends on both the dog and the handler. A protection dog is not simply purchased; it has to be matched to a person who understands the responsibility of owning and maintaining a serious working dog.

features: Continued development to the program standard

paragraphs: A client doesn't necessarily have to wait until a dog is finished and pay the full placement price in one transaction. When I have a dog that has made the program and I believe there's a suitable match, the client can reserve during development — I know who I'm preparing the dog for, and they can follow that development as it takes place. The relationship begins before handover, not on delivery day.
Once a dog is matched to a future handler, later work can also be adapted to that person's environment and requirements without lowering the standard.
